title: Diagonalizing a matrix
overview: A matrix can mix coordinates even when the underlying transformation acts by simple stretching. An eigenbasis reveals those directions. In that basis the transformation is diagonal, which turns repeated matrix multiplication into powers of scalars.

decisions.situation: Find a direction preserved by a transformation
decisions.approach: Look for a nonzero vector satisfying $Av=\lambda v$.
Find $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors over the chosen field.

decisions.situation: Compute repeated applications of a diagonalizable matrix

essentials.title: Order matters
essentials.text: The eigenvalue in each diagonal position of $D$ must correspond to the eigenvector in that column of $P$.

blocks.text: An eigenvector of $A$ is a nonzero vector $v$ satisfying $Av=\lambda v$. The scalar $\lambda$ is its eigenvalue. An eigenbasis is a basis consisting of eigenvectors.
Being able to find one eigenvector tells us about a single direction. To describe every input using such directions, we need enough independent eigenvectors to span the space.
An $n\times n$ matrix over a field is diagonalizable over that field precisely when it has $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors there.

blocks.title: Construct the diagonalization
steps: Find an eigenbasis; diagonalization requires $n$ independent eigenvectors.
Put those eigenvectors in the columns of $P$.
Put their eigenvalues in the same order on the diagonal of $D$, then write $A=PDP^{-1}$.
blocks.text: Column by column, $AP=PD$. Since the columns form a basis, $P$ is invertible.

blocks.title: An upper triangular matrix
blocks.text: For $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$, take $v_1=(1,0)^T$ and $v_2=(1,1)^T$. Multiplying gives $Av_1=2v_1$ and $Av_2=3v_2$. In this basis, $D=\operatorname{diag}(2,3)$.
For a positive integer $k$, successive factors of $P^{-1}P$ cancel, leaving $A^k=PD^kP^{-1}$. Only the diagonal entries of $D$ need to be raised to the power $k$.
